explain.say: In 1086 William the Conqueror's officials surveyed England, village by village, counting land, ploughs and pigs. The result, the Domesday Book, still sits in The National Archives at Kew in London. It is a primary source, made at the time. But every source was made by someone, for a reason. The chain on the board is your toolkit for questioning it.

draw.text: Primary sources and archives: questioning evidence and hearing the silences

explain.say: First, sort sources. A primary source comes from the time you study: a letter, a census, a photograph. A secondary source is a later account built from primary ones, like a textbook. Look at the two groups. Here is a tricky one for you: is a 1950s history book primary or secondary? It depends on your question!

Back to the chain. Ask who made it and why. Domesday was made so the king could tax and control his new kingdom. That purpose shapes what it counts and what it ignores. Historians call this provenance, which means where a source comes from. Why might a tax record make people look poorer than they were?

explain.say: Archives are everywhere. Look at the map: The National Archives in London, the Torre do Tombo in Lisbon, the National Archives of India in New Delhi, and the manuscript libraries of Timbuktu in Mali, where families saved hundreds of thousands of old manuscripts. In 2012 and 2013 people smuggled many of them to safety during the war. Who decides what an archive keeps?

The last link asks what is missing. The Haitian scholar Michel-Rolph Trouillot showed in Silencing the Past, 1995, that silences enter at every stage: what was written, kept, found and told. Great job. Your challenge: pick one family document at home and run all five questions on it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary source?
faq.a: A primary source was made during the period you study, like a letter, law or photograph. A secondary source is a later interpretation built from primary sources, like a textbook or article. The same item can be either, depending on your question.
asks: Is a textbook a primary source?

faq.a: An archive is an organised collection of records kept because of their lasting value, such as government papers, church registers or family manuscripts. Archives are selected and arranged by people, so they have their own history and biases.
Provenance is where a source came from: who made it, when, where, for whom and why. Knowing it lets you judge how reliable and how biased the source may be.
asks: Who made it and why does it matter?
How do historians check a source?

faq.a: Gaps in the record. Enslaved people, women, peasants and colonised peoples often left few documents, or appear only through the eyes of officials. Michel-Rolph Trouillot showed that silences enter when sources are made, kept, found and turned into history.

faq.q: Are primary sources more reliable than secondary sources?
faq.a: Not automatically. A primary source can lie, exaggerate or be mistaken, and a good secondary source compares many primary ones. Reliability depends on the question and on careful checking.

facts: The Domesday Book of 1086 is held by The National Archives at Kew, London.
Michel-Rolph Trouillot published Silencing the Past: Power and the Production of History in 1995.

quiz.say: You study the 1950s and read a history textbook written in 1955 to see how people then saw the war. What is that textbook for you?
quiz.show: A 1955 textbook, used to study 1950s attitudes, is a…
quiz.why: Used as evidence of 1950s views, the textbook comes from the period you study, so it is a primary source.

wrong.1: It would be secondary if you used it only for facts about the war itself.
wrong.2: Every piece of evidence can be classed by how you use it.

quiz.say: Why was the Domesday Book made?
quiz.show: Why was the Domesday Book made in 1086?

options.show: To record the king's resources for tax and control
options.say: To record the king's resources for tax and control

options.show: To tell the story of the Battle of Hastings
options.say: To tell the story of the Battle of Hastings

quiz.why: William's officials recorded land, ploughs, animals and value so the crown knew what it could tax and who held what.

wrong.1: Domesday is a survey, not a narrative of the conquest.
wrong.2: It records land and resources, not religious belief.
